week.t: NASA: Artemis III becomes a rehearsal, landings move to 2028
Roman telescope passes checkout, enters final commissioning
Psyche fires up for the asteroid belt
Malaria parasite caught breaking into a blood cell

tiles.cap: NASA's next giant telescope passed checkout. It sees 100 million times fainter than you.
tiles.nums: fainter than the human eye can see: Roman’s Wide Field Instrument
tiles.p1: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has finished its checkout and moved into science commissioning: test observations that calibrate its instruments and sharpen image quality before real science begins. Senior project scientist Julie McEnery says the observatory is fully functional. NASA adds that some systems are performing even better than required.
tiles.p2: Thursday’s update. Meanwhile Hubble has been photographing gravitational lenses to get Roman’s map ready.
deep: The crowded-field worry
One concern was that Roman’s guidance system might struggle to lock onto stars in crowded star fields and dusty nebulae. Operations project scientist Tom Barclay reports those tests went well.
Why tiny flaws matter

Josh Schlieder, the Wide Field Instrument scientist, says image flaws must be minimised because small imperfections could hide faint signals. The instrument can detect objects about a hundred million times fainter than the human eye can see.
Hubble is drawing the map

Hubble photographs one gravitational lens at a time; Roman’s much wider view should catch a far larger sample. Astronomers are using Hubble’s sharp images to build a computer model for analysing Roman’s big pictures, and Hubble will follow up on the interesting lenses Roman finds.
What a lens tells you

In one Hubble image, an elliptical galaxy about 4.5 billion light-years away bends the light of a galaxy about 8 billion light-years away into an arc, with a smaller flipped copy on the other side. Visible matter cannot account for the bending, so the distortion lets researchers work out how much dark matter the foreground galaxy holds.

tiles.cap: NASA’s Psyche is crossing to the asteroid belt with its engines on nearly 90% of the time.
tiles.nums: of thrust from xenon ion engines, running nearly 90% of the time until 2029
tiles.p1: After a Mars gravity assist, Psyche has fired its electric thrusters nearly non-stop since 28 September, pausing once a week to check in with Earth. The Hall-effect thrusters push with up to 250 millinewtons by firing out xenon ions, and navigation lead Don Han says they will run nearly 90% of the time until arrival.
tiles.p2: Target: a metal-rich asteroid about 280 km across thought to be the partial core of a planetesimal, a building block of an early planet. Orbit by summer 2029.
deep: Fuel
It launched in October 2023 with about 1,090 kg of xenon and has used roughly a third in three years.
Powered by sunlight

Two five-panel solar arrays with 75 square metres of collecting area run the thrusters. Propulsion engineer Steve Snyder says they fire at full power for three months, then throttle down to about half as sunlight weakens further out.
The twist problem
The swirling ions give the spacecraft a slight twisting force. Reaction wheels absorb it, and periodic manoeuvres dump the built-up momentum.
Why Mars first

Principal investigator Lindy Elkins-Tanton says the Mars flyby let the team calibrate instruments and rehearse for the asteroid encounter. Her line: “cruising with confidence deeper into the solar system, powered by sunlight”.

tiles.cap: Ingenuity flew 0.7 km in one go. New blades could take a Mars helicopter 18.7 km.
tiles.nums: in one uninterrupted flight, carrying scientific instruments
tiles.p1: NASA Ames, with Imperial College London and Nagoya University, designed a thinner, asymmetrical rotor blade shape called roamx-0201 using simulations tuned to Mars conditions. In wind tunnel tests it performed better and recovered better in risky flight conditions. Ingenuity, the first powered aircraft on another planet, could cover 0.7 km in one flight; the new blades could stretch that to as much as 18.7 km.
tiles.p2: Paper published 22 September. Not Mars-ready yet: engineers are still closing the gap between what the computer predicts and what the wind tunnel shows.
deep: The speed-of-sound wall
The speed of sound is lower on Mars than on Earth, so rotor tips approach it sooner and performance drops suddenly. The new blades run longer at higher speeds before that happens.
Tripping the air on purpose
The airfoil deliberately disrupts the boundary layer of air at its leading edge, which NASA says lifts the rotorcraft more effectively than earlier designs.
Stall
Ingenuity’s blades lost performance steeply at stall. Under the conditions tested, roamx-0201 behaved much better, which could let future helicopters fly safely across a wider range of angles.
What flies next
SkyFall, due to launch in 2028, carries three helicopters to Mars with curved-edge blades like Ingenuity’s. The new shape is meant for the missions after that.

tiles.cap: Your computer can’t make a truly random number. Two boxes 30 m apart just did, provably.
tiles.nums: between the two quantum devices: too far for any signal to cross in time
tiles.p1: Computers make “random” numbers from a formula and a starting seed, so an attacker can sometimes guess them, and the encryption keys built from them. Physicists at ETH Zurich led by Renato Renner used quantum events instead, which are random by nature, and produced numbers whose randomness they can prove with only a vanishingly small chance of error.
tiles.p2: “When randomness is weak, the keys built from it become guessable,” says former NSA cryptographer David Holtzman.
deep: Two flawed boxes make one perfect one
Each device has small hardware flaws that bias its output, but the two biases are unrelated. A mathematical “randomness extractor” combines the two streams so the flaws cancel.
Why 30 metres

The devices ran at the same moment in separate places, 30 m apart, so not even light could carry a signal from one to the other before each outcome was recorded. Each measured a quantum event, such as a photon passing through a light-splitting device.
The Bell test

To check the result, the team ran a Bell test, which shows a quantum outcome was not faked or planned in advance. Passing it means nobody has to trust that the devices are perfect: “device-independent” proof. Published in Nature on 27 May 2026.
An idea from 2012

Renner and a colleague proposed the method in 2012. A 2025 team at JPMorgan Chase claimed certified randomness by assuming no classical computer could ever copy its result; Renner says his result “does not require any [limits] on the capabilities of someone trying to predict the randomness”.

tiles.cap: The = sign was invented in 1557 by a man tired of writing “is equal to”.
tiles.nums: Robert Recorde’s The Whetstone of Witte, where = first appears
tiles.p1: Early maths was written in sentences: “Ship one brought two hundred fish to port”, then the flounder, bream, sharks and anchovies, one by one. Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde chose two parallel lines of equal length for “equals”, reasoning that no two things can be more equal. His first example was 14x + 15 = 71.
tiles.p2: The × sign is even younger: William Oughtred, 1631. So 5 × 4 = 20 would have made no sense to anyone before then.
deep: What = actually says

Maths historian Clemency Montelle says the equal sign does not ask you to calculate anything. It says one side is identical to the other “even if they don’t look the same”, like 4 + 1 and 5. Think of a balance scale with the same weight on both pans.
Unknowns before x
Ancient Indian mathematicians used abbreviations for colours to stand for unknowns. Ancient Mesopotamians used words meaning length, width and area.
Why astronomers loved them

Before equations, astronomers tracked planets, Moon phases and eclipses with enormous tables of numbers built by hand. An equation is compact: put in a date and a planet’s position, get out the distance it travelled. Montelle says equations “reveal a hidden structure or numerical pattern”.
Plus and minus came first
+ and − came into use in the late 1300s and early 1400s, well before =. Robin Wilson, author of Sum Stories (2025), calls the older sentence-style maths “rhetorical algebra”.

tiles.cap: A raindrop that slides off a leaf picks up a charge. Then it eats through metal.
tiles.p1: Physicist Zhongyuan Ni at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research dripped hundreds of water drops onto copper and saw nothing. He left one experiment running; when he came back the copper looked different. His team then compared drops that had slid along leaves or building materials, picking up an electric charge, with drops placed directly: under a microscope every surface hit by charged drops was damaged. The charged water had eaten through a Teflon coating and begun corroding the copper beneath. Uncharged drops did nothing.
tiles.p2: Ni says the effect is small, no cause for alarm, but it adds up over years on cars, ships, monuments and machinery.
deep: Why copper and Teflon
Copper resists corrosion better than many metals and Teflon is a strong protective coating, so damage there is a hard test. Copper and gold under polystyrene, another coating, showed the same effect.
Where drops get charged
In clouds, or by sliding along a windshield, a leaf, glass or a building. The charge can then pass into materials with the right electrical properties, metals included.
What was known before
Scientists knew drops wear structures down by pounding them, and that rain can carry small amounts of corrosive compounds such as acids. It was not clear whether the charge itself does damage.
What it could change
Stefan Weber, a physicist at the University of Stuttgart not involved in the work, says the finding could lead to better anti-corrosion coatings. Published in Nature on 10 September.

tiles.cap: The malaria parasite was caught breaking into a blood cell. It takes under a minute.
tiles.nums: deaths a year from malaria, almost 150 years after the parasite was first identified
tiles.p1: To get inside a red blood cell, the Plasmodium parasite builds a ring called the moving junction, which briefly opens a gap in the cell’s membrane and closes it so fast that nobody could image it. Chi-Min Ho’s lab at Columbia University caught it with cryo-electron microscopy: three proteins form a dense wedge under the host membrane, a fourth ties the wedge to the parasite, and the wedge shoves the membrane’s lipids aside until the parasite slips through and the membrane reseals.
tiles.p2: The whole break-in takes under a minute, which is also the problem: a drug aimed at it has a window of about 60 seconds.
deep: First seen in 1880
French physician Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran identified the parasite in 1880. Malaria still kills about 600,000 people a year.
Blocking the door
Ho’s team used an AI-designed protein to jam the moving junction. It stopped invasion in test tubes; it has not yet been tested in animals for safety or effect.
Cousins use the same trick
Related parasites such as Toxoplasma and Cyclospora appear to use similar invasion machinery.
Next
The team plans to image other protein complexes involved in infection, including the sticky proteins that keep infected cells from reaching the spleen.

tiles.cap: A*STAR made fat-free whipped cream from pea pods. The foam held its shape for an hour.
tiles.nums: overrun, the volume gained by whipping, for the pea-pod cream
tiles.p1: Siew Bee Ng’s team at A*STAR was washing snap peas when they noticed the peas released a sticky liquid that formed bubbles on the surface. Snap peas are eaten pod and all, so they tested the whole pod as a protein source. At neutral pH the pea protein concentrate matched egg white’s foaming capacity and beat mung bean protein at emulsifying.
tiles.p2: The likely foaming protein is RuBisCO, the abundant leaf protein at the centre of photosynthesis.
deep: How a protein holds a bubble
When whipped, RuBisCO unfolds at the boundary between air and water and links into an elastic network that stops bubbles popping or merging. It was enriched in the foam layer.
Why bother
Plant proteins could replace egg white and dairy proteins in aerated foods like whipped cream and meringue: sustainable, and allergen-free.
The numbers
A fat-free whipped cream made with the extract reached 255% overrun and held its shape for one hour. Protein concentration and whipping speed still need tuning for more air and more stability.
Published
Food Hydrocolloids, 2026. Highlighted by A*STAR Research on 16 October.

tiles.cap: Sunday’s PSI fell to 91–107. Today’s forecast: 70–100, with showers.
tiles.p1: Showers fell over parts of Singapore on Sunday, and the smoke over Kalimantan stayed put instead of drifting here. By 7pm the 1-hour PM2.5 was 25 to 46 µg/m³, Band 1 (Normal), and the 24-hour PSI 91 to 107, down from 108 to 151 on Saturday.
tiles.p2: With winds from the southwest or west and more showers expected Monday to Wednesday, NEA expects the haze situation to keep improving.
deep: Two numbers, two jobs
NEA’s rule: use the 1-hour PM2.5 for what you do right now, and the 24-hour PSI forecast to plan ahead. Band 1 means normal activities for everyone, including children and the elderly.
What the satellite could not see
Fires show up to satellites as hotspots, but on Sunday NEA said the full extent of the hotspots and smoke could not be determined because of cloud cover.
Wind is the whole story
Smoke reaches Singapore only when the wind carries it here. With winds expected from the southwest or west, NEA says the haze risk should be lower.
The weekend in numbers
Friday 85–108. Saturday 108–151, Unhealthy. Sunday 91–107. Monday forecast 70–100.

tiles.cap: Papua New Guinea is heading for its highest fire emissions on record. The smoke stays low.
tiles.nums: days in a row without rain in the Trans-Fly region of Papua New Guinea
tiles.p1: Fires set by people spread across New Guinea through September and October while an El Niño drought dried the island. The VIIRS instrument on NOAA-20 caught thick smoke pouring off the south of the island on 11 October. By 17 October Papua New Guinea’s fires had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon, more than any other year on record at that point, and the Indonesian side more than 35, third after 2015 and 1997.
tiles.p2: Fire scientist Guido van der Werf says 2026 is “very likely” to beat 1997 as Papua New Guinea’s record year. Wet-season rains usually arrive in early November.
deep: Why the smoke hurts
NASA’s Robert Field: “a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems.” Flights were delayed and cancelled, and in some areas children and older people were told to wear masks.
How a managed fire escapes

Fires are commonly lit for crop burning, pasture, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting. In a drought they run out of control, especially in the drier south, where some areas have had only 5 to 10 percent of normal rain since August.
A new frontier

Papua lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double 2024 and the most since 2017, according to Global Forest Watch. Yang Chen of UC Irvine calls it “Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier”.
Why Sumatra is quieter
Sumatra’s fires are relatively low, partly because so much of it is already developed; Field says most fire happens in unmanaged areas or at the edges of primary forest.

tiles.cap: NASA just rewrote the Moon plan. Artemis III won't land. It will rehearse.
tiles.p1: On Friday NASA announced that Artemis III, launching in 2027, stays in Earth orbit: Orion docks with a Blue Origin test lander, then a SpaceX Starship test ship, to check every system before anyone tries the surface.
tiles.p2: The actual landings near the Moon's south pole are now set for 2028.
deep: Three rockets, one mission

Blue Origin's Blue Moon test lander launches first into a 273-mile orbit, where it can wait up to 30 days. Orion follows on SLS days later, climbs to about 345 miles, and after two days of checks docks with it. The crew spends about two days aboard, evaluating the lander's systems.
Then Starship

SpaceX launches a Starship Version 3 test article into a lower orbit. Orion docks with it for up to two hours. Nobody goes aboard; the point is to prove the two ships can find each other, talk, and hold together.
Who flies
Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas and ESA's Luca Parmitano. After the dockings they have up to five more days of tests in orbit, then splash down off California.
Why rehearse

NASA wants to prove the capsule and the landers can meet, dock and work together before trying it at the Moon. A problem 345 miles up means coming home in hours; at the Moon, 239,000 miles away, it means days.

tiles.cap: Satellites say this El Niño now rivals the monster of 1997
tiles.nums: chance it stays strong into early 2027 (NOAA)
tiles.p1: NASA put 2026's ocean next to 1997 and 2015 using 35 years of sea-height measurements. The shape matches 1997: a tilt of warm, high water stretching to South America. This one arrived faster, and JPL's Josh Willis says it is on track to be even bigger.
tiles.p2: 1997-98 brought heavy rain and floods to California, and fires to Indonesia.
deep: Measuring heat with a ruler
Warm water expands. Satellites that bounce radar off the sea can measure its height very precisely, so a bulge in the eastern Pacific is a direct reading of stored heat.
Three satellites, one record
TOPEX/Poseidon measured 1997, Jason-2 measured 2015, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich measures now. They fly almost the same track, so the maps compare cleanly.
What it means for us
For Singapore the pattern is typically drier, hotter, hazier. The haze tile on this wall is the first instalment.

tiles.cap: An AI proved a cousin of the hardest problem in maths
tiles.p1: The Riemann hypothesis is a 167-year-old question about how primes are spread. On 6 October an AI settled the "quasi-Riemann hypothesis", a softer version, and human experts have checked it.
tiles.p2: Mathematicians are split between "staggering" and "what's left for us?"
deep: The problem
Primes look random, but the Riemann hypothesis says their spacing follows a hidden pattern tied to a function called zeta. Proving it has resisted everyone since 1859 and carries a $1 million prize.
What the AI did

On 6 October OpenAI released hundreds of machine-written papers. One proved the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a strictly weaker statement that still says a lot about primes. Earlier AI claims had holes; this one has been checked line by line by mathematicians at Stanford and elsewhere and stands.
Why mathematicians are rattled

Some call it the biggest AI-for-maths result so far. Others ask what a mathematician's job is if machines can find and prove deep results. Quanta ran a piece titled 'Is AI the end of math as we know it?'
Your angle
Olympiad-style problems are now routine for these systems. The skills that still matter are choosing which question to ask and knowing when a proof is beautiful rather than merely correct.

tiles.cap: Stare at this and your eyes will invent a colour
tiles.p1: Your three colour sensors tire out separately. Wear out green, look at white, and you see a magenta ghost. That's an afterimage.
tiles.p2: Then mix red, green and blue light yourself in the PhET simulator.
deep: What's happening in your eye

Your retina has three kinds of cone cells, roughly for red, green and blue. Stare at one colour and the cones for it get fatigued and fire less. Look at white, and the other two shout louder, so you see the opposite colour.
The test
Look at the white dot in the green disc for 30 seconds without moving your eyes. Then look at a blank white wall. You should see a magenta disc that follows your gaze and fades over several seconds.
Try variations
Stare at red and you see cyan. Stare at blue and you see yellow. Half-cover the shape and the ghost has a hard edge. Blink and it jumps.
Mix light yourself
Red + green light = yellow. All three = white. Your screen does this with every pixel.

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at Penn put it in six words. Hand the boring, repetitive stuff to the machine. Keep for yourself anything you want to become good at, and anything you enjoy. His colleague Trent Cash at Waterloo adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient and AI will not turn our brains to mush. It is a choice, made daily.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. When it was switched off, they found fewer than before. Three months was enough for the skill to fade.
The readers who gave up

People who worked through SAT reading questions with AI help were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because sticking with a hard question is itself the skill.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
tiles.src: Science News Explores · Cash et al. 2026 · Lira Luttges et al. 2026

tiles.cap: Make it be wrong, then catch it
tiles.p1: Three habits the researchers say build skill instead of eroding it. One: attempt the problem first, even badly, then ask. Two: ask the AI to argue the opposite of what you think. Three: paste in your own answer and ask it to find the mistake, instead of asking for the answer.
tiles.p2: A fourth for fun: ask it a question you already know the answer to, and see how confidently it gets it wrong.
deep: Why this works
Every one of these keeps the thinking on your side of the screen. The AI becomes a sparring partner, not a vending machine.
Score yourself
For a week, note each time you used an AI: was it before or after your own attempt? The before-count is the one to shrink.
Tell Dad what you find
Use the box at the bottom of this wall. If one of these habits turns out useless, say so; the researchers would want to know too.
